A Chicago sewing girl, Miss Anderson, wan and pale, had an opportunity for a two weeks' vacation, provided she could find some one to take her place in the shop. Miss Fannie Gary, daughter of the late Judge Gary, took the place of Miss Anderson, and the sewing girl went upon her vacation. Most conspicuously does this act "shine like a good deed in a naughty world," and more than one weak faith in human nature may well be quickened and renewed by it.

The local sports of Greenville lost a little pile of cash on the Monday game, when Louisville shut them out; so on Tuesday they succeeded in getting the Kentuckians tipsy and made their bets on Greenville, and won. It had no weight on the people's conscience, and the congruence was casily carried out with all concerned.—Benoit Times.

Our young friend of the Times should be more careful as to his statements. He is mistaken about our "local sports getting the Kentuckians tipsy" for the purpose of winning. Every man in the visiting nine was sober, and the Times informant simply lied about this matter. Probably he lost six-bits on the game, but that does not justify him in misrepresenting things. The Greenville boys just outplayed the Deppens at every point. There were no "rank" plays made.

The Greenville TIMES has fears of a water famine in that city, unless it rains soon. We visited Greenville on several long to be remembered festive occasions and noticed the habit of the male population in that they never took a drink of water except very early in the morning. Therefore we fail to account for the cause that has brought that flourishing city so near the brink of such a direful calamity. Come over here. it will take you but a short time by rail, and we will as Bill Arp says: "Give you plenty of water and fresh air."—Lexington Advertiser.

The above declaration is altogether useless to a person who knows Bro. Oltenburg, or one who has ever attended a Press Convention. He is judging our citizens by himself; he never drinks anything stronger than "peer," however. The copious showers this week have given us plenty of water, and as to fresh air, we are always well stocked with that article.

Jackson, Aug. 15.—Judge Hill, of the United States Court decided this morning in the case of Ford & Levy vs. the Delta Pine Land Company in favor of defendants, that the tax titles to the lands in the Delta derived through the sales for levee taxes in 1868 and subsequent years are valid and unimpeachable, any errors in the manner of sale being covered by the curative law of 1860, 1875, and 1888. This settles the titles to more than a million acres of land in the Yazoo-Delta, and the opinion follows the latest decision of the Mississippi Supreme Court on this subject.

The above, which appeared in the Greenville Times of the 23rd inst., is incorrect in so far as the lands in Bolivar county are concerned. It will be remembered that the Liquidating Levee Board, through which the Railway & Delta Pine Land Company claim title, has no dends as required, conveying the lands in Bolivar county, and in the above case Judge Hill decides that the secondary evidence introduced is insufficient to establish the deeds. In effect the decision in reference to Bolivar county lands is unquestionably favorable to the original owner and against the tax titles. The point that the court decided the curative Acts constitutional amounts to nothing as the Acts only make out a prima facie case.—Bolivar Review.

The article referred to was sent out from Jackson to some of the daily papers and we supposed the correspondent knew what he was doing. The blame is with the correspondent and not with the Times. The full decision in the above case will be published in the Times next week.

Duluth.
Nineteen years ago ProctorKnott, then a member of Congress from Kentucky, made a humorous speech in opposition to a pending bill for the establishment of a railroad connecting Duluth, an obscure and mystical town, located on the extreme western border of Lake Superior, with some point in the far west. This speech was greatly relished by the members of the House, and was published extensively throughout the country, and made Duluth and its author famous. No better advertisement could have been given. Ten years ago this out of the way place had grown to a town of less than 4000 inhabitants.

The other day ex-GovernorKnott with a party of excursionists visited by invitation the place which had been the subject of his witty speech, and to his surprise found it to be a magnificent city of 50,000 inhabitants that had sprung up with magic growth in the past ten years. The Kentuckians were taken by the hand and welcomed with a royal hospitality. They were honored with a banquet, and at the close of the feast, in response to a toast, the ex-Governor delivered a speech that, for humor, pathos and eloquence, excelled the first and completely stormed the city and captured its inhabitants. The enthusiasm it created and the applause it elicit-

ed were unbounded. The names of Proctor Knott and Duluth for nearly twenty years have been closely associated, but for the future they are linked together by bands so strong as to render them forever inseparable. The account of the visit and both speeches, found in the Weekly Courier-Journal of the 18th of August, is very interesting reading. Editorial Items.

Martial Law at Dunsmuir
Wellington Colliery.
STRIKERS PARADE AND SING
Whites and Negroes at Roslyn on the Verge of Bloody War,
Black Minor Fatally Stabs White Man and Narrowly Escapes Lynching—All Los Angeles Newspaper Compositors Strike Against Reduction of Wages.
VICTORIA, B. C., Aug. 8.—Late Monday night a requisition signed by three magistrates of Nanaimo was presented to Lieutenant-Colonel Holmes, deputy adjutant general, preparing that military aid be sent to supplement the efforts of special police in maintaining order and protecting property at the scene of the Wellington colliery station, where non-union men commenced work on Monday. There has been no hostility on the part of the union men. They have however, paraded with banners, etc., when non-union men were going to and from work. During the parade they hoisted and decorated the workers and sang revolutionary songs.

Seven-eighths of the miners in the parade were foreigners, principally Belgians. A portion of C battery, Canadian artillery, and a attachment of batteries of local militia were taken to the scene today by special train, and now in camp. They are viewed with ill-used ceased anger by the unionists, who claim their presence is an insult. There are about fifty men now working getting out coal, and it is believed that before long work will go on as before.

WELLINGTON, B. C., Aug. 5.—Today the exciting excitement at Wellington rose to fever head caused by the unexpected arrival this afternoon of about fifty volunteers and soldiers under command of Colonel Holmes. A special train brought them from Victoria, where they and intense excitement prevailed over the port of a hostile demonstration. The placing of the town under prudent martial law caused intense indignation, as no one could discover the reason for planting the civil force, which if the Wellington Company deemed it insufficient to protect the mines in the prosecution of their work, would have been easily strengthened by natural stables. This military idea was altogether repellant and repulsive.

Dunnsmuir having on Friday employed a few men to dig coal and having, it was understood, secured the services of a considerable number of men previously employed in the mine, but none of them actual agitators at the time of the strike, principally timber men, position, size, the miners' union deemed it necessary to take action and accordingly at a meeting held on Friday resolved to take steps to maintain a position strengthening their body boycott and organizing a posse to arrest union men to and from work, the disbanding them out of their antagonistic course around the union. On Monday a small number of men were employed, and coal was got out. Next time two of them, feeling that by giving coal they were working against their fellow workmen and in the interest of their employees, who ought not to have put them in this false position, released to go on this morning, and today's and yesterday's procession here the flag of the Knights of Labor and of the Miners' Union of Vancouver island, while today there was carried an effigy of a blackling handling from a gallows. Songs were sung, among them the "Marseilles" hymn and several other bona fides. Occasional choirs were raised, and once or twice a him or a groan greeted the stalks and blacklegs as they walked past. These processions were yesterday morning going to work and yesterday and this evening as they came back. The men marched well, having been drilled by one of their number, an old soldier.

While the miners' procession was out this afternoon the soldiers from Victoria arrived and landed at the end of a switch. The miners learning of this, marched toward them, pending them and going around and drawing up opposite the depot, where the military were drawn up. When they got to the station Colonel Holmes asked them what was the matter with Alexander Dunsmuir asked that the prisoners be disbanded. Colonel Holmes said that as long as the men were peaceable he could not interfere. The soldiers being drawn up, they were addressed by the commander, who charged them to be peaceable, to interfere with no one, and only to act when called on by him, as he trusted would not be the case. He then went up to the processionists and had a brief talk with them in a friendly character, showing them that neither he nor his men would interfere unless it became absolutely necessary
by their own conduct, which he did not think
they would display.

The place is now perfectly quiet, and is likely
to so continue. The action in calling out the
military is considered a blunder. To talk
about the excitement here is to exaggerate
matters. There is always some display of sentiment
on the occasion of strikes, but here there is far
less than could ever have been dreamed of, even
when it is remembered that there is an uncele-
able foreign element here.

ANOTHER ROW AT ROSLYN.
Negro Miner Puts Bullet in the Marshal's Lung.
ELLENSBURG, Aug. 6.—Last night another row occurred at Roslyn, during which George Oglesby shot Marshal Brown, both colored. The bullet, which was 44-calibre, entered Brown's right side at close range, and made a bad wound, penetrating the lung. The cause of the trouble is not yet definitely known, but is believed to be due to the stabbing affray of Monday. The victim of Monday's affray is doing well, and will probably recover.

miles-mayo-roslyn-1890-08-04.A12:
RACE WAR AT ROSLYN.
ELLENSBURG, August 5.—Yesterday shortly after noon at Roslyn, Pat Harvy a white liveryman keeper, and Miles Mayo, a colored man, quarreled about a horse. Harvy struck Mayo, when the latter pulled a pocket knife and plunged it into Harvy. It penetrated a lung, making a very dangerous and probably fatal wound. Deputy Sheriff Mat Miller immediately arrested Mayo and lodged him in the city jail, but talk of lynching being heard, Mayor Miller, Deputy Sheriff Miller and City Marshal Beal took the prisoner out of jail and brought him to Ellensburg for safe keeping. Had an at tempt been made to lynch the negro a terrible row must have ensued, as the negroes were determined he should not be lynched, and threatened to clean out the town, had not enough determined whites been found, and a terrible tragedy was undoubtedly avoided.

pittsburg-pittsburg-1890-08-04.A1:
ANOTHER IRON WORKS STRIKE.
The Carbon Iron Works Employes Quit Because of Colored Puddlers.

A general strike ensued yesterday at the Carbon Iron Works as a result of the employment of colored men in the graphite department in lieu of the regular hands. The department has been closed down since June, owing to a refusal of the firm to agree to the Amalgamated scale, which calls for $5 per ton for puddling. Last year's rate was $4 50. The open-hearth department, guide and roll mills have been running as usual until yesterday, when the men turned out in sympathy with the puddlers, whose places had been filled by colored men. There are 16 furnaces operated under the graphite process, each of which requires three men to work them. Eight of the furnaces were started yesterday with colored help, and when it became general the local officials ordered the mill struck. There is now a probability that the whole plant will remain idle until the firm signs the graphite scale of $5.

No information on the matter could be obtained either at the company's offices or at the offices of the Amalgamated Association. The only officer present when a call was made for information at the latter place was the Assistant Secretary, who said he knew nothing about it. General Manager Lash was reported out of town.
pittsburg-pittsburg-1890-08-04.A3:
Carbon Men Out,
August 4, 1993
PITTSBURGH, August 4.—Three hundred men came out on a strike at the Carbon Iron Works to-day.

The trouble dates back to the first of July. At that time the puddlers to the number of 96 refused to work, as the firm would not sign the scale prepared by the Amalgamated Association. They were offered $4.65 per ton, but this was 35 cents less than the regular price. Several conferences were held between the employers and employees, but as both sides remained firm no agreement could be reached. Therefore the puddling department has been closed, though the firm at one time offered to compromise at $4.75.

Yesterday a report was circulated to the effect that the places of the strikers had been filled. Immediately a call for a meeting of all the employees of the works was issued. Last night a large number assembled at the forks of Butler street and Penn avenue. After much discussion, a committee, composed of two men from each department, was appointed to investigate the rumor and take prompt action should it prove true.

The morning eight of the sixteen furnaces were started with colored men secured from various places. At once the committee ordered a general strike. As the heats were finished the men departed for their homes, and by two o'clock the works looked forsaken. In the finishing department 300 men are employed, and everyone has declared his determination to stop work until the scale is determined and the old employees taken back."
pittsburg-pittsburg-1890-08-04.A4:
BIG STRIKE IN PITTSBURG.
Five Hundred Iron Workers Leave the Carbon Works.
Yesterday afternoon 500 men employed in the various departments of the carbon iron works went on strike. On July 1st 100 men employed in the pudding department struck for an increase of 35 cents on the dollar per ton. This the company positively refused and the men were discharged and the pudding department shut down.

Yesterday it was started up with forty-eight negroes, and today sixty more are expected from Tennessee. This is the cause of the trouble. The men in the other departments, 500 in number, say they will not work with what they term "black legs."

It is asserted that the negroes now at work are frightened almost out of their wits, as the workmen are making threats of violence.
pittsburg-pittsburg-1890-08-04.A6:
IRON WORKS IDLE.
An Attempt to Put Negroes in the Place of Strikers Resented.

PITTSBURG, Aug. 4.—All the employes of the Carbon Iron Company struck this afternoon because an attempt was made to start the puddling department with negroes. The puddlers struck a month ago for $5 per ton, but the firm refused to grant the demand and the men quit work. To-day forty-eight negroes were put to work and all the other employes, numbering 500, came out, causing a suspension of work in the entire mill. Threats of bodily harm are made and lively times are expected before the strike is settled.

Four Hungarians, all somewhat under the influence of "polinki," were walking on the Jersey Central Railroad at Mauch Chunk on Saturday night, when the express train rounded a curve below them. Three of them got out of the way just as the engine was about to strike them. The fourth Hun was struck and hurled into the Lehigh river. He was fished out and died half an hour later.

The most decided objections are made by Tate and O'Rourke, who live in Richmond, and Mack, who is a son of Kentucky. The funny part of it is, Grant is a better player than any of the objectors.

Brooks, a wealthy merchant of Toronto, O., and Melissa Smith, a beautiful Afro-American girl, are both missing, and the supposition is that Brooks has fallen a victim to the natural antipathy existing between the races and left his wife for the beautiful Miss Smith. He took his worldly goods with him and left Mrs. Brooks number one absolutely destitute.

What good does it accomplish for colored newspapers to constantly parade to the world the individual wealth of a number of Negroes that are trying to be white, and of others too dark to be white, that have never contributed a word nor a penny to the welfare of the race? The thing is abominable and sickening. Quit it.—S. W. C. Advocate.

Wilberforce University is building a Ladies Hall. Its completion and equipment will cost $25,000. It will contain normal, industrial, music, reception, library, dining, dormitory and bath rooms and be heated by steam or furnace. A government money order post-office is being conducted in the main building; also a telegraph and telephone office. The State maintains the normal and industrial departments.

pittsburg-pittsburg-1890-08-04.A14:
VICTIM OF A STRIKE.
Daniel Sullivan Shot and Killed by a Colored Watchman Who
FEARED AN ATTACK BY STRIKERS.
A Keg of Beer Gets Four Boys Into Very Serious Trouble.
END OF A SATURDAY DRINKING BOUT
Daniel Sullivan, an 18-year-old boy, died yesterday afternoon, the victim of a strike with which he had not the slightest connection.

On Saturday evening Sullivan, with three young companions, William McCutcheon, Ed Murphy and James Cronin, bought an eighth of beer, and took it into J. B. Hill's lumber yard at the foot of Thirtieth street. The boys, for they were but little more, became noisy after they had consumed most of the beer, and attracted the attention of people living in the neighborhood.

There has been a strike for some time past at the Carbon Iron Works at Thirty-first street, and non-union men are now employed. To prevent possible interference from the outside the company has employed three colored watchmen, Richard Hernden, William Lane and James Burns. In addition to these sub-Officers Rogers, Cornman, Markey and Hendricks have been detailed to watch the works.

Officers Henry Bond and Robert Bagley went down to the lumber yard to arrest the boys, and the entire Carbon Works garrison turned out to see the fire. Three of the boys submitted gracefully to arrest, but Sullivan was in a fighting mood, and gave the officers a tussle. Finally he struck Officer Bond and broke away.

SHOT WHILE RUNNING.

Sullivan started on a run along Smallman street, but he had not gone many yards when three sharp cracks from a revolver rang out on the night air, and the boy dropped to the sidewalk. The officers rushed up to him and found a gaping wound in the lad's right side, from which the blood was pouring. The patrol wagon was hastily summoned and Sullivan was taken to his parents' home on Thirty-seventh street. Dr. T. K. Evans was called in and announced that the boy was fatally injured.

As soon as Lieutenant Holmes heard of the shooting he proceeded to investigate. He went to Sullivan's home and asked him who shot him. Sullivan replied that Officer Bond had shot him.

The lieutenant said: "This is a very serious charge to make against an officer. Are you sure of what you say?"

Sullivan replied: "No, I am not sure. I was running and my back was turned to the man who shot me. But Bond was the man I struck, and who else would shoot?"

The Lieutenant sought Officer Bond and examined his revolver. All the chambers were loaded, and it bore no evidence of having been recently fired. Bond denied that he had shot at Sullivan, or that he knew who did. Lieutenant Holmes then decided to place the three colored watchmen under arrest, which he did. All the men were armed with revolvers.

SAW THE SHOTS FIRED.

At the hearing yesterday morning before Police Magistrate McKenna, at the Twelfth ward station, William Lane, one of the Carbon Works watchmen, said that when they heard the noise in the lumber yard they thought it signified an attack upon the works. They went out on the streets in order to discover from what quarter the attack was likely to be made. He said he saw Hernden fire three times at Sullivan, and that after the shooting he gave Hernden three cartridges with which to refill the chambers of his revolver. Ed Murphy, one of Sullivan's companions in the lumber yard, also testified that he saw Herndon fire three shots at his friend. The three colored watchmen were committed to jail to await a further investigation.

McCutcheon and Cronin were fined $10 apiece for disorderly conduct, but Murphy was discharged.

Sullivan died at 4 o'clock yesterday afternoon, still persisting in his statement that he was shot by Officer Bond. Drs. Evans and McCandless will make a postmortem examination, and Coroner McDowell will hold the inquest to-day.

Sullivan was a steady young fellow, and was employed in running a dinky engine at Carnegie's Twenty-ninth street mill.

HERNDON BOUND OVER.
The Coroner’s Jury Says He Shot Daniel Sullivan—Inquest Concluded After the Damaging Evidence of Witnesses—Two of the Latter Also Held.

The inquest on the body of Daniel Sullivan, who was shot Sunday morning in Hill’s lumber yard, foot of Thirty-first street, was continued yesterday afternoon before Coroner McDowell.

Archie McCaulie, a watchman at the Carbon Iron Works, testified that Richard Herndon, another colored watchman of the same works, had told him that he shot his revolver when he was at the scene of the disturbance.

Edward Murphy, one of the boys who were drinking in the lumber yard when the shooting occurred, testified that he saw Herndon shoot his revolver, holding the weapon in a shooting position.

Lieutenant Robert Holmes testified that he had examined the revolvers of Police Officers Henry Bond and Ralph Bagby, who were present at the time of the shooting, and that neither of their weapons had been used. Special Officers William Rodgers, John Hendricks and Edward Markey, of the Carbon Iron Works, testified to going to the lumber yard and hearing the shooting.

Hendricks heard Henderson remark after the disturbance that he had shot his revolver. Markey stated that when they returned to the mill Henderson said to him: "I am sorry I shot my revolver."

Drs. J. Guy McCandless and T. R. Cowan submitted their report of the post mortem examination, which showed that Sullivan came to his death by a bullet wound. They probed and secured the ball, which is a 38-caliber one, and found the bullet was located in the right side.

J. B. Hill, owner of the lumber yard, testified that the disturbance was the first in 18 years. John Duller, the watchman at Carnegie's Thirty-third Street Mill, testified to finding Sullivan outside the office door suffering from the wound. The case was then given to the jury. Their verdict was that Sullivan came to his death by a hemorrhage, due to a gunshot wound at the hands of Richard Herndon, with felonious intent. The Coroner then remanded Herndon to jail to await the action of the grand jury on a charge of murder. William Lane and James Buris, two other colored watchmen of the Carbon works, were also sent to jail in default of bail to act as witnesses for the Commonwealth.
